## Purpose

An integration operation files *delegate* tasks so someone does a piece of its
work: a verifier for a branchless parent aggregate, a repair-stage writer, a
candidate-member resolver. When the operation ends — cancelled by an operator,
superseded by a newer generation, or completed without ever needing that
delegate — the ticket is obsolete. Nothing schedules it, nothing waits on it,
and nobody will ever close it.

This settles those tickets for **one** operation. `aq integration abort` already
releases as it cancels, so this exists for operations that ended before that
shipped, or that completed without their delegate. The fleet-wide equivalent is
`aq doctor --check integration.stranded_delegates --fix`; both run the same code
in `src/integration/delegate_release.py`.

## When a playbook uses it

It does not. This is an operator control, LOCAL authority only, reached through
`aq integration release-delegates OPERATION_ID`.

## How it works internally

`IntegrationRecoveryControls.release_delegates` locks the operation, refuses it
unless its state is `completed` or `cancelled`, and calls
`release_delegates_on` inside that transaction. For each delegate of the
operation that has not settled and has no live writer — no assigned agent, no
session that is anything but fully stopped — it:

1. force-transitions the ticket to `FAILED`, context
   `integration_delegate_retired`;
2. writes `integration_retirement` task metadata (operation, state,
   disposition, previous status/attention/hold, cleanup);
3. clears the holds a cancellation left (`needs_attention`,
   `claim_prepare_backoff_until`, `blocked_terminal`, `manual_pause`);
4. inserts an `integration_delegate_releases` audit row;
5. logs `task.updated`.

## Side effects and persistence

Terminal `FAILED` on each released ticket, `integration_retirement` metadata,
and one durable `integration_delegate_releases` row per release. That row
carries no foreign key to `tasks` or to the operation, so it survives deleting
or archiving the task it describes.

It never manufactures a pass, never touches branches, stage evidence or retry
counters, and never releases a retained branch owner or workspace lock — those
are preserved exactly as found and reported as named cleanup blockers, which
`aq task explain <task-id>` re-reads live.

## Failure modes and diagnostics

| Outcome | Cause | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| `not_found` | No operation with that id. | `aq integration status PROJECT_ID` lists the live ones. |
| `invalid_state` | The operation is `active`, `escalated` or `human_required`. Its delegates are its own business. | Stop the operation first: `aq integration abort OPERATION_ID --reason "..."`. |
| `nothing_to_release` | The operation ended and every delegate has already settled, or the only unsettled one still has a live writer. | `aq doctor --check integration.stranded_delegates` shows what is left and why. |
| `released` | Settled at least one ticket. | `released_delegates` names them; `integration_delegate_releases` records why. |

## Example step

Not used from a playbook. From an operator shell:

```bash
aq integration release-delegates repair-batch-integration-batch-2c48…
```
